title: async-serialization-and-retry-guidelines-2024
author: Elena Park
content:
Title: Async Serialization and Retry Guidelines for Inference Clients

Summary:
This document prescribes standardized patterns for asynchronous request serialization, client-side backpressure handling, retry semantics, and deterministic payload shaping for Redwood Inference SDKs and internal services. The goal is to reduce flakiness, avoid head-of-line blocking in streaming paths, and ensure reproducible inputs to the serving runtime while preserving low-latency behavior and clear observability signals.

Scope:
- Redwood public SDKs (Python, TypeScript, Go) and internal service-to-service inference clients.
- Applies to both streaming and non-streaming API surfaces (text generation, chat, embeddings).
- Does NOT replace transport-level TLS, authentication, or platform networking rules.

Owner and Contacts:
- Owner: Elena Park (SDK Platform)
- Reviewers: Miguel Alvarez (Runtime), Sasha Li (SRE)
- Related teams: eng-serving-runtime, eng-platform, eng-sre, eng-developer-experience

Design principles (why these rules exist):
1) Non-blocking I/O: Client libraries must favor non-blocking async APIs for streaming endpoints to avoid head-of-line blocking of unrelated requests.
2) Deterministic serialization: Payload serialization must be deterministic for a given logical request to allow stable telemetry aggregation and reproducible debugging.
3) Explicit backpressure: Clients must communicate local backpressure to upstream (retry/admission) mechanism where applicable and expose a consistent metric for queued bytes/frames.
4) Idempotent-by-default semantics: Retries should be safe for common patterns; where not safe, explicit opt-in with idempotency tokens is required.

Recommended patterns (summary):
- Use stream-friendly encodings: newline-delimited JSON (NDJSON) or explicit length-prefixed frames for streaming.
- Canonical field ordering for JSON payloads produced by SDKs to ensure deterministic byte sequences.
- Local client queue size and time thresholds with observable metrics and a documented eviction policy.
- Exponential backoff with capped jitter, bounded retry budget, and explicit idempotency tokens for non-idempotent calls.

Detailed guidelines:
1. Serialization rules
  a. Canonical JSON schema: SDKs must produce canonical JSON for requests: keys sorted lexicographically, consistent floating-point formatting (6 decimal places by default), and omission of null fields. Example (Python canonicalization snippet):

  ```python
  import json
  def canonicalize(obj):
      return json.dumps(obj, separators=(",",":"), sort_keys=True, ensure_ascii=False)
  ```

  b. NDJSON for streaming: For streaming tokens or events, use NDJSON where each line is a complete event frame. Avoid embedding raw newlines in token frames; if needed, escape using base64 with accompanying content-type metadata.

  c. Length-prefixed binary frames for high-throughput services: When binary payloads are used, adopt a 4-byte big-endian length prefix followed by the payload. Include a one-byte type tag if multiple frame kinds are possible.

2. Async API surface and ergonomics
  a. Public SDKs must expose both synchronous (blocking) and idiomatic asynchronous APIs (async/await in Python/TS, goroutines in Go) for streaming endpoints. The async API must implement backpressure-aware consumers (async iterators/streams).

  b. Example TypeScript streaming consumer pattern:

  ```ts
  for await (const chunk of client.streamResponse(req)) {
    // backpressure-aware: processing can yield to event loop
    await processChunk(chunk)
  }
  ```

3. Backpressure and local queuing policy
  a. Clients MUST cap the local queued messages/bytes per connection. Default caps: 2MB per-connection queued payload and 1,000 event frames. These defaults are tunable via client config.

  b. Eviction policy: LRU for cached frames, oldest-first drop for queued requests with documented metrics exposed (client.queue.drops, client.queue.size_bytes).

  c. Metric requirements for SDKs and services (table):

  | Metric name | Type | Cardinality | Description |
  |-------------|------|-------------|-------------|
  | client.queue.size_bytes | gauge | per-client | Current queued bytes waiting for send |
  | client.queue.drops | counter | per-client | Number of queued messages dropped due to capacity |
  | client.send.latency_ms.p90 | histogram | per-endpoint | Time to send request to transport |

4. Retry semantics and budgets
  a. Retry types: immediate-retriable (transient network errors), delayed-retriable (rate-limits / 5xx), and non-retriable (4xx client errors).

  b. Idempotency: By default, generation calls are considered non-idempotent. SDKs must expose an idempotency token parameter: if provided, retries for the same token may be retried safely by server semantics. For higher-level convenience, client helpers may generate deterministic tokens derived from canonicalized request hash for idempotent-safe modes.

  c. Retry policy defaults:
  - Max attempts: 3
  - Initial backoff: 100ms
  - Multiplier: 2.0
  - Max backoff: 2s
  - Jitter: full jitter (randomized between 0 and backoff)

  d. Retry budget: Per-client sliding window budget: no more than 10% of requests may be retried in a 60s window by default. Servers and gateways may enforce this budget; clients should surface throttling to callers via well-defined exceptions.

5. Observability and error signals
  a. Trace spans must include canonicalized request hash (GUID) as an attribute named request.canonical_hash to correlate retries and instrumentation without logging full payloads.

  b. Error taxonomy: SDKs should map transport and server errors into the standard error classes defined in /confluence/architecture-and-standards/api-standards/typed-error-model-and-client-contract-recommendations-2026. Use those classes for metrics and for user-facing exceptions.

6. Compatibility and migration guidance
  a. Rolling change pattern for serialization schema changes: add-only fields or new optional enum values. When removing or renaming fields, use a two-release deprecation window: (1) client emits both old+new keys with a deprecation header; (2) server removes support.

  b. Backwards compatibility test: unit test matrices must include: canonicalization invariants, streaming frame roundtrip, jitter behavior reproducibility in deterministic-mode (seeded random).

Operational runbook (when things go wrong):
1) Symptom: sudden increase in client.queue.drops or client.send.latency_p95 > 2x baseline
   - Step 1: Verify SDK version rolling deployment; check change logs for serialization changes.
   - Step 2: Check telemetry: request.canonical_hash collision rate and server-side validation rejects.
   - Step 3: If caused by a new serializer change, roll back clients to last good version and open an incident titled "serializer-regression-<region>-<time>".

2) Symptom: high retry rates causing downstream cost surge
   - Step 1: Inspect retry budget usage and trace spans for request.canonical_hash to identify hot keys.
   - Step 2: Temporarily reduce client retry multiplier to 1.2 and enable stricter per-client retry budget at gateway.

Acceptance criteria for SDKs (pre-release checklist):
- Canonicalization unit tests with 100% deterministic outputs for representative payload sets.
- Backpressure metrics instrumented and exported by default.
- Retry policy configurable and defaulted to the values in this doc.
- Examples in README for streaming iteration patterns.

Appendix: sample canonicalization test vectors
- Input: {"prompt": "Hello\nWorld", "temperature": 0.7}
- Canonicalized JSON: {"prompt":"Hello\nWorld","temperature":0.700000}
